Rubber Stamp Duke

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet Bruce Murray: 12th Duke of Atholl: businessman, head of a private army, and... a South African.

Unique Selling Point:
Under normal circumstances, an interview with a member of the UK's landed gentry wouldn't inspire much excitement. But, Bruce Murray's story is anything but normal. As the 12th Duke of Atholl, able to raise the UK's only "private army", he has collected more titles than he can remember. He also happens to be a South African who, when not rubbing shoulders with Britain's "mink and manure" set, runs a humble rubber stamp business in Louis Trichardt.

Summary:
This insert tells the story of Bruce Murray, the 12th Duke of Atholl. It will include a visit to the family's estate at Blair Castle in the Scottish Highlands, where his two sons, Michael and David, will take the salute on the Duke's behalf from the Blair Highlanders. This infantry regiment constitutes the only legal private army in the UK -an honour bestowed on the family by Queen Victoria. We have been granted permission to film at the castle by the estate's Trust, which includes a rare go-ahead for the use of a drone. Michael and David have also made themselves available for interviews.

Further filming will be done in Louis Trichardt, where we'll film an interview with Bruce and the rest of the family. The juxtaposition of the Highlands and Limpopo should add additional texture to the piece.

Further information:
Because of the distances to be travelled, this shoot will require two days of filming. A frying session has been arranged to discuss how best to arrange the logistics, as well as how best to structure the piece given its two very distinct locations.

A local camera operator has already been sourced, and a UK travel budget drawn up.

Extra Budget Items:
Potentially some archive footage depending on what the family has available, as well as additional car hire and accommodation for the Louis Trichardt shoot.

Press Release:


The Rubber Stamp Duke
Outside the British Royal family, being a Duke or Duchess is at the very top of the British aristocratic pyramid and it’s a title that South African Bruce Murray could never have imagined. But the businessman, who runs a humble rubber stamp business in Louis Trichardt, now finds himself at the head of the only private army in Europe, and the 12th Duke of Atholl. With his historic seat at Blair Castle in the Scottish Highlands, Murray sits comfortably amongst the UK’s upper crust.


Script:


Duke of Atholl Final Script:
VO: This is Bruce George Ronald Murray. As the South African commander of an unlikely foreign army, he once came eyeball-to-eyeball with the Queen of England.
ITV Bruce Murray: (00:35:20:10) The Queen’s people told us what would happen the moment we presented our colours to her, and then they said after that we can’t advise you. It will depend entirely on what she does… and this is when I realised that she’s just another human being because we looked each other into the eye and she was as confused as I was about what to do next and she was sort of looking to her left and right, there was nobody there to advise her and I was obviously feeling extremely tense and there was this palpable and quite long silence of us sort of raising our eyebrows at each other. Eventually I said mam may I please the regiment off. And she said with pleasure colonel and that was how we dealt with it.
VO: How he came to share a moment of awkwardness with the world’s longest reigning living monarch is down to an unlikely quirk of fate. One that has forever bound two countries or, more specifically, two towns on opposite ends of the planet – one in the Scottish Highlands, the other in the northern reaches of Limpopo.
Link: Go back a couple of hundred years and Louis Trichardt was a Voortrekker settlement. These days its one of the larger towns on the trek to or from Zimbabwe and according to my Satnav its 9417kms from Blair Atholl in Scotland. Which is probably unsurprising, except these two towns have more in common than you might think.
(Pause)
Down a side road in the centre of Louis Trichardt stands this humble rubber stamp and sign-making business. Its owner is none other than Bruce Murray: father of three, biker and outdoor enthusiast. Oh, and Chief of the Clan Murray, 12th Duke of Atholl.
Upsound: (00:32:54:02) It’s such a rare privilege, we refer to it as an accident of birth which is exactly what it is. Absolutely no control over your birth and mine was as it is, and it’s enriched it incredibly (cut) I have met people and done things and seen things that I would never have done otherwise.
VO: Blair Atholl: A small village 114km north of Edinburgh. Population: a little over 500 (566; 1991). It’s also the closest hamlet to a castle that is... well, a little magical.
Within these whitewashed walls has unfolded 750 years of history. It’s the seat of the Chief of Clan Murray and, had events unfolded a little differently, it might have been where Bruce Murray called home away from home. But, it’s no longer under the control of the Duke, and is managed as a self-funding enterprise by a charitable trust.
In 1996, this man, Iain Murray, the 10th Duke of Atholl died a committed bachelor.
Some reversing and sharp turns through the family tree revealed the next in line for the title to be a distant cousin. Not only that, but a distant cousin whose parents had set sail from England to settle at the southern tip of Africa.
John Murray was by then already in his late 60’s and, according to his son Bruce, not overly keen on joining the Scottish nobility.
ITV: Bruce Murray: [00:02:52.00]… My father just was overwhelmed by the possibilities of what his duties would be. That he might have to go there as well. And he actually made applications to abdicate if that’s the right word. Anyway, it turns out that a member of the nobility can’t actually abdicate unless you have been involved in a schedule 1 offence or die. That’s the only way. and then your title goes to your successor. So there was no ways that he was going to be able to get out of it.
Link: Each of the 12 Dukes had their own personality and impact on the Castle and Estate. But, there would have been a little concern when the title passed to the 11th Duke, a South African. And it’s fair to say he did things a little differently.
VO: John Murray brought a common touch to his time as Duke, often arriving unannounced at people’s homes for a catch up. He became known as the People’s Duke. Not bad for a man who confessed to not being a fan of whiskey.
ITV: Bruce Murray: [00:02:52.00]… when he did become the 11th duke he did a really good job of it. He was a duke for 15 years and he went every single year, bar the last year before he passed away. He was 86 when he died so he did his last trip when he was 85…
VO: John Murray died on the 15th of May 2012 and was buried in a small cemetery in Haenertsburg, in Limpopo. His title passed to Bruce, his eldest son, who became the 12th Duke of Atholl.
Over tea and snacks at his home in Louis Trichardt, Bruce confides that, despite knowing he’d one day inherit the title he remained nervous about doing the wrong thing.
COFFEE ITV: Bruce Murray (15:37:26:12)… The scope of putting one’s foot in it is massive.
Question (Off Camera) And have you done that?
COFFEE ITV: Bruce Murray (15:37:30) Probably, I’ve probably shut it out of my memory out of sheer horror. But luckily there are also some very eccentric people there. You know, the previous adjutant (CUT) who is also a neighbour of the estate just said, “don’t worry about it, you’re the Duke you can do whatever you want to”.
He was, though, far more comfortable taking on another weighty responsibility of Dukedom, the one that years later would bring him face-to-face with the Queen.
Link: The history of Blair Castle is full of dramatic twists and turns, but none more so than a visit by Queen Victoria in 1844. It was on that trip that she gave permission for the establishment of the Atholl Highlanders…
VO: Now a regiment of roughly 100 men – the Atholl Highlanders had been around for a long time. Drawn from the local community, they were what these days might be known as bodyguards. After Queen Victoria gave her stamp of approval, they became and remain Europe’s only private army. With the Castle and the estate now in private hands, leading the Highlanders has become the Duke’s primary responsibility.
A significant responsibility too for these men who, hours before today’s annual Highlanders’ parade, were to be found putting the finishing touches to uniforms not entirely suited to the unusually hot Scottish weather. Nor, it seems, entirely suited to people who like to dress buy themselves.
ITV: Michael Murray ([00:00:33.00] No, it is a bit of a process. We've got what’s called a plaid which need two people to put on but again its quite a uniform to put on. So, the officers meet for a lunch beforehand and we get a few men in and they sort of help us get dressed before the lunch.
VO: On the morning of the parade, Michael Murray and his brother David are a mixture of excitement and anxiety.
ITV: David Murray [00:02:26.07]: I actually do get a little bit nervous every time. I'm calling the command for the first time this year so there is a lot that can go wrong... you know if your voice suddenly gets squeaky and you shout a command back to the xxx command, it’s not going to look good. So, I am a little bit nervous this year.
VO: Nervous, too, perhaps that they’re representing their father, the 12th Duke, who hasn’t made the trip this year. It’s a sign that this regiment – so dependent on the backing of the Duke – will be in good hands for at least another generation.
ITV: Mike Murray (00:11:09:01): It’s very dear to us as well, it’s important to keep it going and in the right way as well, so not commercial (CUT) It’s a tradition that everyone, it’s sort of close to their hearts and they do it because it is so special really
ITV: David Murray (00:11:31:04): It is and it’s entirely unique. It is the only privately-owned army in Europe, and it would be such a shame to lose that tiny slice of history.
VO: But there’s something else that makes this particular private army unique – something that hasn’t escaped its commanding officer back in Louis Trichardt.
COFFEE ITV: Bruce Murray (15:45:05): The Atholl Highlanders as a unit have never fired a shot in anger, you know which is quite remarkable because they’ve maintained this wonderful military history but they’re not a…
Question (behind camera): They’re not what you’d call a fighting force.
ITV: Bruce Murray: No (laughs)
VO: Fighting force or not, their annual parade remains a significant event in Blair Atholl and the surrounding Highlands.
(Pause)
Keren Guthrie is the archivist at Blair Castle. It’s her job to ensure the preservation of history. More than that, though, she’s one of the Atholl Highlanders’ biggest fans.
ITV: Keren Guthrie: (00:07:03:02): it just gets to your heart. Even if you have no connection to the Murray Family or to the Castle. I defy anyone not to feel that in their hearts. I get the shivers. The pipes, the drums, and to watch the soldiers parade is just wonderful.
VO: It’s hard to know if each of the men taking part in the parade felt the burden of 100’s of years of history and tradition, or if all of them thought about the absent Duke. What is clear, is that two of them certainly did.
ENDS.
